source_refs.note: Exercise 14.3, Question 1 (i)-(iv): a x b and b x a by the determinant formula, checked by dot products (book p.282). Answer key PDF 312.

blocks.prompt: 1 (i) Compute the cross product \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) and \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\). Check your answer by showing that each \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\) are perpendicular to \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) and \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\). \(\underline{a} = 2\underline{i} + \underline{j} - \underline{k}\), \(\underline{b} = \underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}\).
blocks.explanation:
A cross-product computation.
We must find \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) and \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\) and check them.
Plan: determinant for \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\), change all signs for \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\), then two dot products.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{a} = 2\underline{i} + \underline{j} - \underline{k}\), \(\underline{b} = \underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}\).
To find: \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) and \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\), then check perpendicularity.
Method: The determinant formula of 14.3.5 gives \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) from the components; \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a} = -(\underline{a} \times \underline{b})\); a dot product of 0 shows perpendicularity.

Write the determinant
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Row 1 holds the unit vectors, row 2 the components of the first vector \(\underline{a}\), row 3 those of the second \(\underline{b}\). The order of the rows follows the order of the product.

Work out the three minors
\[\underline{i}\text{ minor} = (1)(1) - (-1)(-1) = 0\]
\[\underline{j}\text{ minor} = (2)(1) - (-1)(1) = 3\]
\[\underline{k}\text{ minor} = (2)(-1) - (1)(1) = -3\]
Why: For each unit vector cover its row and column; the minor is (top-left)(bottom-right) minus (top-right)(bottom-left).

Attach the signs \(+, -, +\)
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \underline{i}(0) - \underline{j}(3) + \underline{k}(-3)\]
\[= -3\underline{j} - 3\underline{k}\]
Why: Expanding a determinant along row 1 uses the sign pattern \(+, -, +\); the middle (\(\underline{j}\)) term is subtracted.

Find \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\)
\[\underline{b} \times \underline{a} = -(\underline{a} \times \underline{b})\]
\[= 3\underline{j} + 3\underline{k}\]
Why: Swapping the two vectors swaps rows 2 and 3 of the determinant, and swapping two rows changes the sign. So the cross product is not commutative: \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a} = -(\underline{a} \times \underline{b})\).

Check: \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\) are perpendicular to \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\)
\[\underline{a} \cdot (\underline{a} \times \underline{b}) = (2)(0) + (1)(-3) + (-1)(-3)\]
\[= 0 - 3 + 3 = 0\]
\[\underline{b} \cdot (\underline{a} \times \underline{b}) = (1)(0) + (-1)(-3) + (1)(-3)\]
\[= 0 + 3 - 3 = 0\]
Why: Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is 0. Both are 0, so the cross product is correct.

Check with \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\)
\[\underline{a} \cdot (\underline{b} \times \underline{a}) = -\,\underline{a} \cdot (\underline{a} \times \underline{b}) = 0\]
\[\underline{b} \cdot (\underline{b} \times \underline{a}) = -\,\underline{b} \cdot (\underline{a} \times \underline{b}) = 0\]
Why: \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\) is just \(-(\underline{a} \times \underline{b})\); a minus sign does not change a zero dot product. So both vectors are perpendicular to \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\) as well.
blocks.final_answer: \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = -3\underline{j} - 3\underline{k}\), \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a} = 3\underline{j} + 3\underline{k}\); both dot products are 0, so \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\) are perpendicular to both.

blocks.prompt: 1 (ii) Compute the cross product \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) and \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\). Work out the three minors
\[\underline{i}\text{ minor} = (3)(1) - (2)(-1) = 5\]
\[\underline{j}\text{ minor} = (1)(1) - (2)(2) = -3\]
\[\underline{k}\text{ minor} = (1)(-1) - (3)(2) = -7\]
Why: For each unit vector cover its row and column; the minor is (top-left)(bottom-right) minus (top-right)(bottom-left).

Attach the signs \(+, -, +\)
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \underline{i}(5) - \underline{j}(-3) + \underline{k}(-7)\]
\[= 5\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} - 7\underline{k}\]
Why: Expanding a determinant along row 1 uses the sign pattern \(+, -, +\); the middle (\(\underline{j}\)) term is subtracted.

Find \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\)
\[\underline{b} \times \underline{a} = -(\underline{a} \times \underline{b})\]
\[= -5\underline{i} - 3\underline{j} + 7\underline{k}\]
Why: Swapping the two vectors swaps rows 2 and 3 of the determinant, and swapping two rows changes the sign. So the cross product is not commutative: \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a} = -(\underline{a} \times \underline{b})\).

Check: \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\) are perpendicular to \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\)
\[\underline{a} \cdot (\underline{a} \times \underline{b}) = (1)(5) + (3)(3) + (2)(-7)\]
\[= 5 + 9 - 14 = 0\]
\[\underline{b} \cdot (\underline{a} \times \underline{b}) = (2)(5) + (-1)(3) + (1)(-7)\]
\[= 10 - 3 - 7 = 0\]
Why: Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is 0. Both are 0, so the cross product is correct.

Check with \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\)
\[\underline{a} \cdot (\underline{b} \times \underline{a}) = -\,\underline{a} \cdot (\underline{a} \times \underline{b}) = 0\]
\[\underline{b} \cdot (\underline{b} \times \underline{a}) = -\,\underline{b} \cdot (\underline{a} \times \underline{b}) = 0\]
Why: \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\) is just \(-(\underline{a} \times \underline{b})\); a minus sign does not change a zero dot product. So both vectors are perpendicular to \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a}\) as well.
blocks.final_answer: \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = 5\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} - 7\underline{k}\), \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a} = -5\underline{i} - 3\underline{j} + 7\underline{k}\); both dot products are 0, so \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\) are perpendicular to both.
